sections.heading: What is doxycycline used for?
sections.body:
Doxycycline is an antibiotic, a medicine that treats or prevents certain infections caused by bacteria. In the UK it is available only with a prescription. The NHS lists chest infections, dental infections and skin infections among the problems it treats, together with rosacea, sexually transmitted infections and some rarer infections. It can also be used to prevent malaria in people travelling abroad, and people taking it for that reason are not expected to feel any different.

MedlinePlus adds that it is used for acne, where it acts on the bacteria in the pores and lowers the amount of oil on the skin.

sections.heading: How does doxycycline work and how is it taken?
sections.body:
Doxycycline belongs to the tetracycline group of antibiotics. The NHS explains that it stops bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive. In rosacea, MedlinePlus describes a different benefit, a reduction in inflammation of the skin. With most infections people usually start to feel better within a few days, while rosacea responds more slowly and is normally reviewed by a doctor after some weeks.

Doxycycline comes as capsules, tablets and dispersible tablets, which are dissolved in water before they are taken. The NHS describes swallowing capsules and standard tablets whole with water and staying upright for a while afterwards. The NHS says taking it after a meal or snack, or with a drink of milk, may ease feeling sick. The NHS stresses that finishing the whole course matters, even when symptoms have eased.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of doxycycline?
sections.body:
The NHS says the most common side effects are headaches and feeling or being sick. Doxycycline can also make the skin sensitive to the sun. The NHS advises covering up, wearing a hat and sunglasses and using a high-factor sunscreen. NHS England pharmacy guidance also describes avoiding direct sunlight and ultraviolet light, including sunbeds and sun lamps. A fingernail that starts to come away from its base is listed among the serious effects and is linked to a reaction to sunlight.

The NHS lists pain or difficulty swallowing, a sore throat, heartburn and chest pain that worsens with eating as possible signs of an inflamed or ulcerated food pipe. The NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected. Serious allergic reactions are rare, and the NHS says to call 999 if the lips, mouth, throat or tongue suddenly swell or breathing becomes difficult. Other rare effects include inflammation of the bowel, changes in blood cells, liver problems, pancreatitis and raised pressure around the brain.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with doxycycline?
sections.body:
The NHS says doxycycline is usually taken by adults and children over 12, and that younger children can take it for some infections. It can discolour teeth because it binds to calcium in growing bone and teeth. A previous allergic reaction to doxycycline or another medicine, kidney or liver problems, an inflamed food pipe (oesophagitis), lupus and myasthenia gravis are listed as reasons it may not be suitable. The NHS says a penicillin allergy is not a barrier, because doxycycline belongs to a different class of antibiotic.

The NHS does not recommend doxycycline during pregnancy because it can affect a baby's tooth and bone development, although a doctor may still advise it when the benefits outweigh the risks. For breastfeeding, one NHS page says a short course may be possible once a doctor or health visitor has confirmed the baby is healthy, while another NHS page lists breastfeeding among reasons it may not be suitable. Emc product information is stricter and lists pregnancy and lactation as contraindications. The NHS says doxycycline does not stop any type of contraception from working, but being sick or severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours may reduce the protection of contraceptive pills.

sections.heading: Doxycycline with other medicines and alcohol
sections.body: The NHS says anticoagulants such as warfarin, antacids, acne medicines, and iron or zinc supplements may not mix well with doxycycline. The NHS also lists products containing aluminium, bismuth, calcium or magnesium among those to mention to the prescriber, and local NHS leaflets differ on how far apart they should be spaced from doxycycline. Emc product information says systemic retinoids such as isotretinoin should be avoided with doxycycline, because the combination raises the risk of raised pressure inside the skull. With warfarin, emc product information for a doxycycline dispersible tablet reports a longer prothrombin time, a measure of how quickly blood clots. The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with doxycycline because it can stop it working properly. Apart from alcohol, the NHS says people can eat and drink normally while taking it.

faqs.q: Does doxycycline stop contraception from working?
faqs.a: The NHS says doxycycline does not stop any type of contraception from working. The exception is being sick or having severe diarrhoea for more than 24 hours, which may mean contraceptive pills do not protect against pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can people drink alcohol while taking doxycycline?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is best not to drink alcohol with doxycycline, because alcohol can stop it working properly. Apart from that, it says people can eat and drink normally while taking it.

faqs.q: Does doxycycline make skin more sensitive to the sun?
faqs.a: Yes, the NHS says doxycycline can make the skin sensitive to the sun and advises covering up and using a high-factor sunscreen. NHS England pharmacy guidance also describes avoiding direct sunlight and sunbeds.

faqs.q: Can doxycycline be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS does not recommend it during pregnancy because it can affect a baby's tooth and bone development, though a doctor may still advise it when the benefits outweigh the risks. For breastfeeding, one NHS page says a short course may be possible once a doctor or health visitor has confirmed the baby is healthy, while another lists breastfeeding as a reason it may not be suitable.

faqs.q: How quickly does doxycycline start to work?
faqs.a: For most infections the NHS says people usually feel better within a few days, though the full course still matters. Rosacea responds more slowly and is usually reviewed by a doctor after some weeks, and people taking it to prevent malaria are not expected to feel any different.

faqs.q: Can people with a penicillin allergy take doxycycline?
faqs.a: The NHS says people allergic to penicillin can take doxycycline, because it belongs to a different class of antibiotic. A previous allergic reaction to doxycycline itself is a reason it may not be suitable.

flucloxacillin.name: Flucloxacillin
flucloxacillin.summary: A penicillin-type antibiotic, available on prescription, used for infections of the skin and wounds, bone infections and ear infections. It is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to a penicillin, and a serious allergic reaction is an emergency that needs a 999 call. Rarely it can affect the liver, sometimes after the course has ended.
usedFor: Skin and wound infections
Bone infections (osteomyelitis)
Ear infections
Impetigo and infected insect bites, which community pharmacists in England can supply it for under NHS patient group directions
flucloxacillin.howItWorks: Flucloxacillin kills the bacteria that cause the infection. As a penicillin, it works by damaging the cell wall that bacteria need to survive, which human cells do not have.
flucloxacillin.onset: The NHS says most infections should improve within a few days.

common: Feeling sick and diarrhoea are the main common effects, with bloating and indigestion; the NHS says these affect more than 1 in 100 people.
Simple meals and small sips of fluid are suggested by the NHS to help with an upset stomach and to avoid dehydration.
Being sick or having severe diarrhoea can make the combined pill or the progestogen-only pill less reliable, according to the NHS.
serious: Rarely, anaphylaxis (swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, severe breathing difficulty or fainting) is an emergency that needs a 999 call.
Yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes with pale stools and dark urine can signal liver problems; the NHS says to contact a GP or NHS 111 promptly.
Diarrhoea with blood or mucus, blistering or peeling skin, or unusual bruising also needs a GP or NHS 111 contact.
Some of these serious effects, including liver effects, can appear for up to two months after treatment has finished.

cautions: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction to flucloxacillin, another penicillin-type antibiotic or any other medicine as a reason to check with a doctor or pharmacist first.
People with liver or kidney problems, and people who have recently had or are due a vaccination, are also listed for checking first.
Liver injury such as jaundice or hepatitis is a recognised risk; the NHS formulary says it is higher with longer courses and increasing age.
It can make the oral typhoid vaccine less effective.
Medicines to check about include methotrexate, warfarin, gout medicines such as probenecid, voriconazole and other antibiotics.
There is not enough information to say herbal remedies and supplements are free of interaction with it.
Very rarely, taking it with paracetamol has been linked to a blood and fluid imbalance (high anion gap metabolic acidosis).
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking it.
flucloxacillin.monitoring: NHS England pharmacy directions say people taking warfarin or similar anticoagulants should be advised to have their INR monitored during treatment, because rises in INR have been reported.

sections.heading: What is flucloxacillin used for?
sections.body: Flucloxacillin is a penicillin-type antibiotic, and the NHS says it is available only on prescription. It is used to treat infections of the skin and wounds, bone infections known as osteomyelitis, and ear infections. In England, community pharmacists can also supply it for some skin problems, such as impetigo and infected insect bites, under NHS patient group directions. The NHS says most infections should improve within a few days. It also says that carrying on until the prescribed course is finished matters even when a person feels better, because stopping early could let the infection return.

sections.heading: How does flucloxacillin work?
sections.body: According to the NHS, flucloxacillin works by killing the bacteria that cause the infection. As a penicillin, it acts on the cell wall that bacteria need to stay intact, a structure human cells do not have. It belongs to the same family as other penicillin antibiotics. This shared family is why the NHS asks about any past allergic reaction to a penicillin-type antibiotic before it is used. UK patient leaflets say it should not be taken by people with an allergy to penicillin or other antibiotics of the same kind. The leaflets describe swelling of the face, lips, throat or tongue, breathing problems and an itchy rash as signs of a severe allergic reaction, and say to stop the medicine and contact a doctor at once. The NHS says swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, severe breathing difficulty or fainting is an emergency that needs a 999 call.

sections.heading: Taking flucloxacillin
sections.body: The NHS describes flucloxacillin as best absorbed on an empty stomach, meaning it is taken before eating or a good while after a meal or snack. Capsules are swallowed whole with a full glass of water, and the NHS advises against lying down straight after. The medicine comes as capsules, and the NHS also describes a liquid for children and people who struggle with capsules, and an injection that hospitals can give. The NHS says to carry on until the course is finished even when a person feels better, because stopping early could let the infection return. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment. Dosing details are on the NHS medicine page and in the patient leaflet, so they are not given here.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care?
sections.body: The NHS says most adults and children can take flucloxacillin, with a few exceptions to check first. These include a past allergic reaction to flucloxacillin, another penicillin-type antibiotic or any other medicine. People with liver or kidney problems, and those who have recently had or are due a vaccination, are also on the list. In pregnancy the NHS says it can be taken, but a pharmacist or doctor is asked first. For breastfeeding, the NHS says only tiny amounts pass into breast milk, so side effects in the baby are unlikely. The NHS page lists poor feeding, vomiting, diarrhoea, oral thrush or a rash in the baby as signs to look out for and to get advice about.

sections.heading: Side effects and the warning about the liver
sections.body: The NHS says common side effects, affecting more than 1 in 100 people, are feeling sick, diarrhoea, bloating and indigestion. Simple meals and small sips of fluid are suggested to avoid dehydration, and being sick or having severe diarrhoea can make the contraceptive pill less reliable. Serious side effects are rare, affecting fewer than 1 in 10,000 people according to the NHS. They include yellowing of the skin or eyes with pale stools and dark urine, which can point to liver problems. UK leaflets describe jaundice and hepatitis, meaning liver inflammation, as effects that can be delayed for up to two months after treatment ends. An NHS formulary says the liver risk is higher with longer courses and with increasing age. Diarrhoea with blood or mucus, blistering or peeling skin and unusual bruising are also warning signs. For these, a GP or NHS 111 is the route to care, and some can appear after the course has finished. Anaphylaxis is rare but an emergency, with swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, severe breathing difficulty or fainting needing a 999 call.

sections.heading: Taking it with other medicines
sections.body: The NHS says some medicines can change how flucloxacillin works or raise the chance of side effects. Examples it names are methotrexate, warfarin, gout medicines such as probenecid, voriconazole and other antibiotics. Flucloxacillin can make the oral typhoid vaccine less effective, so a doctor is told about a recent or planned vaccine. NHS England pharmacy directions note that rises in INR have been reported with warfarin and similar anticoagulants, and that INR should be monitored. Very rarely, a blood and fluid imbalance called high anion gap metabolic acidosis has been reported when it is taken with paracetamol. The NHS says there is not enough information to say herbal remedies and supplements are free of interaction, partly because they are usually not tested for their effect on other medicines. The NHS lists are examples only, and the leaflet in the pack has the full list.

faqs.q: Can flucloxacillin be taken with food?
faqs.a: The NHS describes it as taken on an empty stomach, which means before eating or well after a meal or snack.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking flucloxacillin?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment. It separately lists yellowing of the skin or eyes as a rare serious side effect.

faqs.q: What should happen if a rash or swelling develops after a dose?
faqs.a: Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, severe breathing difficulty or fainting is a medical emergency, and the NHS says to call 999 straight away.

faqs.q: Can liver problems appear after the course has finished?
faqs.a: UK leaflets and the NHS say serious effects, including jaundice or hepatitis, can appear up to two months after finishing, so yellow skin or eyes with pale stools and dark urine needs a GP or NHS 111 contact.

faqs.q: Is flucloxacillin suitable in pregnancy and breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says it can be taken in pregnancy after checking with a pharmacist or doctor, and that only tiny amounts reach breast milk, so effects on a baby are unlikely.

co-amoxiclav.name: Co-amoxiclav (Augmentin)
co-amoxiclav.summary: A penicillin antibiotic that combines amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, used for bacterial infections such as those of the ears, lungs, sinuses, skin and urinary tract. It is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to it or another antibiotic, or liver problems or jaundice while taking an antibiotic. The NHS lists diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, and thrush as common side effects.
co-amoxiclav.class: Penicillin antibiotic with a beta-lactamase inhibitor
usedFor: Infections caused by bacteria, according to the NHS.
Infections of the ears, lungs, sinuses, skin and urinary tract, as listed by MedlinePlus.
Sinus, bone and joint, and dental infections, according to UK patient leaflets.
co-amoxiclav.howItWorks: Co-amoxiclav is an antibiotic that works by killing the bacteria causing an infection. It contains two medicines, amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. MedlinePlus describes amoxicillin as a penicillin-like antibiotic that stops the growth of bacteria, and clavulanic acid as a beta-lactamase inhibitor.

common: Diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, and thrush are the common side effects listed by the NHS.
The NHS says co-amoxiclav will not usually affect the ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery.
serious: Anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, can cause swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue or fast or difficult breathing, and the NHS amoxicillin page says to call 999 for these signs.
Serious skin reactions can include blistering or peeling skin; the NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected.
Liver problems can show as pale poo with dark pee, or yellowing of the whites of the eyes or the skin; the NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected.
Some UK patient leaflets list inflammation of the large intestine, which causes watery diarrhoea, among the serious side effects; the NHS route for suspected serious side effects is NHS 111.
Pancreatitis, inflammation of the pancreas, causes severe pain in the stomach or back that does not go away; the NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected.

cautions: The NHS says most adults and children can take co-amoxiclav, but it is not suitable for everyone.
It is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to co-amoxiclav or another antibiotic, which can include a skin rash or swelling of the face and throat.
It is not suitable for people who have had liver problems or jaundice while taking an antibiotic, and MedlinePlus asks that past liver problems after taking it be reported to the doctor.
The NHS says co-amoxiclav can usually be used in pregnancy if the doctor thinks it is needed, and usually while breastfeeding after checking with a pharmacist or doctor.
The NHS names gout medicines such as allopurinol or probenecid, warfarin and methotrexate as medicines that may not mix well with it.
MedlinePlus says amoxicillin and clavulanic acid may decrease the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives.

A 2026 NHS Somerset primary care guide advises avoiding broad-spectrum antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav when narrower ones remain effective, because of the risk of C. difficile, MRSA and resistant urinary infections.

sections.heading: What is co-amoxiclav used for?
sections.body:
Co-amoxiclav is an antibiotic, a medicine that treats infections caused by bacteria. The NHS describes it as a penicillin antibiotic for bacterial infections. MedlinePlus says it treats certain infections caused by bacteria, including infections of the ears, lungs, sinuses, skin and urinary tract. UK patient leaflets also list sinus, bone and joint, and dental infections, and note that it has no effect against infections caused by viruses.

The NHS says most adults and children can take it, although it is not suitable for everyone. NHS formularies list it as tablets and as an oral suspension, which is a liquid form, and injection forms also exist. A March 2026 primary care guide from NHS Somerset advises avoiding broad-spectrum antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav when narrower ones remain effective. The reason it gives is the risk of Clostridium difficile infection, MRSA and urinary infections that resist treatment.

sections.heading: How does co-amoxiclav work?
sections.body:
Co-amoxiclav contains two medicines, amoxicillin and clavulanic acid. UK patient leaflets describe it as an antibiotic that works by killing the bacteria that cause infections.

MedlinePlus describes amoxicillin as a penicillin-like antibiotic that works by stopping the growth of bacteria. It describes clavulanic acid as belonging to a class of medicines called beta-lactamase inhibitors. The NHS describes co-amoxiclav as a penicillin antibiotic.

The NHS Somerset primary care guide names co-amoxiclav among the broad-spectrum antibiotics to avoid when narrower ones remain effective. The electronic medicines compendium (emc) publishes separate leaflets for different strengths and forms, and lists Augmentin tablets and suspensions as prescription-only medicines. Leaflets differ between products, so the leaflet in the pack is the reference for a particular medicine.

sections.heading: What are the common side effects?
sections.body:
The NHS lists diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, and thrush as the common side effects of co-amoxiclav. It also says co-amoxiclav will not usually affect the ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery.

The NHS says co-amoxiclav can sometimes cause serious side effects, although most of them are rare. MedlinePlus lists severe vomiting as a warning sign to report to the doctor. A UK formulary notes that cholestatic jaundice, a liver problem that causes yellowing of the skin, can occur during or shortly after use of co-amoxiclav.

The next section describes the serious side effects the NHS lists and the route to care for each.

sections.heading: Which warning signs need urgent help?
sections.body:
The NHS lists four serious side effects: a severe allergic reaction, skin reactions, liver problems and inflammation of the pancreas. Signs of a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) include swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue and fast or difficult breathing, and the NHS amoxicillin page says to call 999 for these.

Serious skin reactions can include blistering or peeling skin. Liver problems can show as pale poo with dark pee, or yellowing of the whites of the eyes or the skin. Pancreatitis, inflammation of the pancreas, causes severe pain in the stomach or back that does not go away. Some UK patient leaflets also list inflammation of the large intestine, which causes watery diarrhoea.

The NHS co-amoxiclav page says to call NHS 111 for anyone taking co-amoxiclav who thinks serious side effects may be happening.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care, and which medicines interact?
sections.body:
The NHS says co-amoxiclav is not suitable for people who have had an allergic reaction to it or another antibiotic, which can include a skin rash or swelling of the face and throat. It is also not suitable for people who have had liver problems or jaundice while taking an antibiotic.

MedlinePlus asks that any past liver problems after taking amoxicillin and clavulanic acid be reported to the doctor, who may advise against taking it again. UK patient leaflets note that some people with kidney problems may need the treatment changed.

In pregnancy the NHS says co-amoxiclav can usually be used if the doctor thinks it is needed. While breastfeeding it can usually be taken after checking with a pharmacist or doctor. The NHS names gout medicines such as allopurinol or probenecid, warfarin and methotrexate as medicines that may not mix well with it. MedlinePlus says it may decrease the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives.

faqs.q: Is co-amoxiclav the same as amoxicillin?
faqs.a: No. Co-amoxiclav contains amoxicillin together with a second medicine, clavulanic acid, which MedlinePlus describes as a beta-lactamase inhibitor.

faqs.q: What are the common side effects of co-amoxiclav?
faqs.a: The NHS lists diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting, and thrush as the common ones. The NHS says co-amoxiclav will not usually affect the ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery, and that most serious side effects are rare.

faqs.q: Can co-amoxiclav cause liver problems?
faqs.a: The NHS lists liver problems among the serious side effects, with pale poo and dark pee or yellowing of the skin or whites of the eyes as signs. It is not suitable for people who have had liver problems or jaundice while taking an antibiotic. The NHS says to call NHS 111 if serious side effects are suspected.

faqs.q: What if the face or throat swells after taking it?
faqs.a: Swelling of the lips, mouth, throat or tongue, or fast or difficult breathing, may be anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, and the NHS amoxicillin page says to call 999.

faqs.q: Can co-amoxiclav be used in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says it can usually be used in pregnancy if the doctor thinks it is needed, and usually while breastfeeding after checking with a pharmacist or doctor.

metronidazole.name: Metronidazole
metronidazole.summary: An antibiotic used for bacterial infections of the skin, mouth and gums, and the vagina and pelvis, and the usual treatment for trichomoniasis. It comes as tablets, liquid, suppositories, gels and creams, and the NHS advises avoiding alcohol during treatment and for 2 days afterwards.
usedFor: Bacterial skin infections and rosacea
Mouth infections, including infected gums and dental abscesses
Bacterial vaginosis and pelvic inflammatory disease
Infected insect bites, skin ulcers, bed sores and wounds
Trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection, which the NHS says is usually treated with metronidazole
metronidazole.howItWorks: Metronidazole is an antibiotic that treats bacterial and parasitic infections. Laboratory studies describe it as being switched on inside susceptible organisms, many of which live without oxygen, by pathways that human cells do not have. Once switched on, it forms short-lived chemical products that bind to DNA and damage it.
metronidazole.onset: The NHS says most infections start to improve within a few days, although the full course is still finished.

sections.heading: What is metronidazole used for?
sections.body: Metronidazole is an antibiotic that the NHS describes as treating several bacterial infections. These include infections of the skin, rosacea, infections of the mouth such as infected gums and dental abscesses, bacterial vaginosis and pelvic inflammatory disease. It can also be used for infected insect bites, skin ulcers, bed sores and wounds. Trichomoniasis, a sexually transmitted infection, is treated with antibiotics, usually metronidazole. It comes as tablets, a liquid to drink, suppositories, skin gel, skin cream and vaginal gel. It can also be given by injection, but this is usually done only in hospital. For most infections, the NHS says people feel better within a few days.

sections.heading: How does metronidazole work?
sections.body: Metronidazole is an antibiotic that treats bacterial and parasitic infections. It belongs to a group of medicines called nitroimidazole antimicrobials. Laboratory studies describe it as being switched on inside susceptible organisms, many of which live without oxygen. The switching-on pathways are absent in the aerobic cells of the human body, which helps explain why the medicine targets microbes. Once switched on, it forms short-lived products that bind to DNA and cause damage, including breaks in the DNA strands.

sections.heading: What are the side effects?
sections.body: The NHS lists feeling or being sick, diarrhoea and a slight metallic taste in the mouth as common side effects of the tablets, liquid, suppositories and vaginal gel. Some people feel drowsy, so the NHS suggests checking reaction times before driving. Metronidazole gel or cream can cause dryness, itching or irritation of the skin. Serious side effects are rare and, according to the NHS, affect fewer than 1 in 1,000 people. Yellow skin or eyes, which the NHS links with liver or gallbladder problems, needs prompt contact with the GP or NHS 111. The NHS lists meningitis and brain disease as very rare serious side effects, and sudden serious symptoms of this kind are an emergency: call 999 or go to A&E. Swelling of the lips, mouth or throat, or trouble breathing, can signal a serious allergic reaction and also needs a 999 call. A hospital factsheet adds that numbness or tingling in the hands and feet can occur with longer courses, a reason to speak to the prescriber.

sections.heading: Metronidazole and alcohol
sections.body: The NHS advises not drinking alcohol while taking metronidazole tablets or liquid or using suppositories. It says to keep avoiding alcohol for 2 days after treatment finishes, while the NHS trichomoniasis page gives at least 24 hours. The reason is that alcohol with metronidazole can cause feeling or being sick, stomach pain, hot flushes, palpitations and headache. The NHS also lists feeling unable to stop drinking alcohol during treatment among the reasons to talk to a doctor before using it. With the vaginal gel, the NHS says drinking can sometimes cause the same effects. MedlinePlus, a US source, gives a longer wait of at least 3 days after the last dose, so advice differs between publishers.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care?
sections.body: The NHS page on who can take metronidazole mentions people who have ever had an allergic reaction to it or another medicine, people who are pregnant or breastfeeding, and people who are having blood tests. Liver problems, dialysis and diseases of the nervous system are further points to tell the prescriber about for tablets, liquid or suppositories. On pregnancy, the NHS says metronidazole may be an option but advises checking with a doctor or pharmacist first. It also says there is no evidence of an effect on fertility in men or women. The Specialist Pharmacy Service says usual courses can be used during breastfeeding, with the baby watched for poor feeding, stomach upset or oral thrush. The NHS says that if sickness or diarrhoea lasts more than 24 hours, the contraceptive pill may not protect against pregnancy.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk during metronidazole treatment?
faqs.a: The NHS advises avoiding alcohol during treatment and for 2 days after finishing, although its trichomoniasis page gives at least 24 hours. Alcohol with metronidazole can cause feeling or being sick, stomach pain, hot flushes, palpitations and headache.

faqs.q: Does metronidazole affect the contraceptive pill?
faqs.a: The NHS says that if sickness or diarrhoea lasts more than 24 hours, the contraceptive pill may not protect against pregnancy. Anyone unsure is advised to ask a doctor or pharmacist.

faqs.q: Can metronidazole be used in pregnancy or while breastfeeding?
faqs.a: The NHS says it may be possible to use it in pregnancy but advises discussing it with a doctor first. The Specialist Pharmacy Service says usual courses can be used while breastfeeding, with the baby watched for feeding problems.

faqs.q: Does metronidazole affect driving?
faqs.a: The NHS says metronidazole can cause drowsiness in some people, so reaction times are worth checking before driving. Anyone who feels drowsy or dizzy may not be fit to drive.

faqs.q: How quickly does metronidazole work?
faqs.a: The NHS says people usually feel better within a few days for most infections. The full course is still finished as prescribed even when symptoms ease.

nitrofurantoin.name: Nitrofurantoin
nitrofurantoin.summary: Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic that the NHS describes as a medicine for lower urinary tract infections such as cystitis, and it is available only on prescription. The NHS lists severe kidney problems, lung conditions and liver problems among the reasons it may not be suitable, and notes that it can turn urine dark yellow or brown, which is harmless.

nitrofurantoin.howItWorks: Nitrofurantoin belongs to a class of medicines called antibiotics, which work by killing the bacteria that cause infection. Like other antibiotics, it has no effect on colds, flu or other infections caused by viruses. The NHS explains that most of a dose is filtered from the blood into the urine, which concentrates the medicine where the bacteria are. West Yorkshire NHS prescribing guidance says it is unsuitable for upper urinary tract infections such as kidney infections.

Dark yellow or brown urine is a common effect that the NHS describes as harmless, and the urine returns to its usual colour once the medicine is stopped
serious: Lung problems are among the uncommon serious side effects; a persistent cough or breathing difficulties need urgent medical advice, and the NHS says to call NHS 111 for a serious side effect other than anaphylaxis
Liver problems such as jaundice (yellowing of the skin or eyes) are uncommon serious effects; the NHS advises calling NHS 111
A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is an emergency that needs a 999 call for an ambulance

G6PD deficiency, liver problems and conditions causing severe weakness are also listed by the NHS as conditions to check

Kidney function is a key check: NHS clinical guidance describes kidney function as a key check and links poor kidney function with the medicine being less likely to reach useful levels in the urine, and the prescriber decides
Pregnancy: the NHS says it can usually be taken earlier in pregnancy, but a doctor may not recommend it later on because it can affect the baby's red blood cells

Breastfeeding: small amounts pass into breast milk and side effects in the baby are unlikely, but the NHS advises checking with a doctor or pharmacist; NHS specialist advice is to avoid it if the infant has G6PD deficiency or jaundice

sections.heading: What is nitrofurantoin used for?
sections.body: Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic that the NHS describes as a medicine for lower urinary tract infections, such as cystitis. It is available only with a prescription. The NHS explains that most of a dose is filtered from the blood into the urine, which concentrates the medicine where the bacteria are. It can also be prescribed to help prevent urinary tract infections from coming back. MedlinePlus places it in a class of medicines called antibiotics, which work by killing the bacteria that cause infection. Like other antibiotics, it does not work for colds, flu or other viral infections. NICE guidance on lower urinary tract infections says nitrofurantoin is not recommended for men with suspected prostate involvement. West Yorkshire NHS prescribing guidance adds that it is unsuitable for upper urinary tract infections, such as kidney infections.

sections.heading: How is nitrofurantoin taken?
sections.body: The NHS says nitrofurantoin is best taken with or after a meal or snack, which helps the body absorb it and helps prevent an upset stomach. Tablets and capsules are swallowed whole rather than chewed or broken. The NHS says a missed dose is skipped if it is nearly time for the next one, and a double dose is not taken to make up for it. The NHS says a doctor should be told if a urinary tract infection does not improve or if symptoms get worse at any time. The NHS stresses the importance of continuing until the course is finished, even after feeling better, to stop the infection coming back.

sections.heading: What are the side effects of nitrofurantoin?
sections.body: The NHS lists nausea, diarrhoea, loss of appetite and headaches as the usual side effects. Dark yellow or brown urine also occurs, and the NHS describes it as harmless. The urine returns to its usual colour once the medicine is stopped. Side effects usually go away when the medicine is stopped, and taking it with or after food can ease nausea. The NHS says serious side effects are uncommon. They include lung problems, liver problems such as jaundice, and allergic reactions. Anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, means calling 999 for an ambulance, while the NHS route for other serious side effects is NHS 111. A local NHS leaflet describes shortness of breath or a lingering cough as lung symptoms needing urgent medical advice, and yellowing of the skin or eyes as a possible sign of liver effects.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with nitrofurantoin?
sections.body: The NHS says most adults and children can take nitrofurantoin, but it is not suitable for everyone. Previous allergic reactions or serious side effects from it, a lung condition, severe kidney problems, diabetes, anaemia, vitamin B deficiency and porphyria are all listed as reasons to check first. The NHS also lists G6PD deficiency, liver problems and conditions causing severe weakness. Kidney function is a key check in NHS clinical guidance. The guidance links poor kidney function with the medicine being less likely to reach useful levels in the urine. Sources differ on the exact kidney-function limit, so the prescriber decides.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, breastfeeding and other medicines
sections.body: The NHS says nitrofurantoin can usually be taken earlier in pregnancy. A doctor may not recommend it later on, because it can affect the baby's red blood cells. Small amounts pass into breast milk and are unlikely to cause side effects in a baby, though the NHS advises checking with a doctor or pharmacist first. NHS specialist advice is to avoid it if the infant has G6PD deficiency or jaundice, because of the risk of haemolytic anaemia. Among other medicines, MedlinePlus lists antacids as a nonprescription product that may interact. NHS pharmacy guidance says magnesium trisilicate may reduce absorption. It adds that products which make urine less acidic, such as some cystitis remedies containing potassium citrate or sodium bicarbonate, can weaken the antibiotic's action. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking nitrofurantoin. MedlinePlus also notes that nitrofurantoin can cause false results on urine tests for glucose.

faqs.q: Why does nitrofurantoin turn urine dark?
faqs.a: Dark yellow or brown urine is a known effect of nitrofurantoin, and the NHS describes it as harmless. The urine goes back to its usual colour once the medicine has been stopped.

faqs.q: Can nitrofurantoin treat a kidney infection?
faqs.a: West Yorkshire NHS prescribing guidance says nitrofurantoin is unsuitable for upper urinary tract infections, which include kidney infections. The NHS describes it as a medicine for lower urinary tract infections such as cystitis.

faqs.q: Does nitrofurantoin work for colds or flu?
faqs.a: No: MedlinePlus says antibiotics such as nitrofurantoin will not work for colds, flu or other viral infections. It is an antibiotic that works by killing the bacteria that cause infection.

faqs.q: Can nitrofurantoin be used in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says nitrofurantoin can usually be taken earlier in pregnancy, but a doctor may not recommend it later on because it can affect the baby's red blood cells. The NHS says the doctor weighs up the benefits and risks with the person.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about kidney problems and nitrofurantoin?
faqs.a: The NHS lists severe kidney problems among the conditions to check before taking nitrofurantoin. NHS clinical guidance describes kidney function as a key check and links poor kidney function with the medicine being less likely to reach useful levels in the urine.

trimethoprim.name: Trimethoprim
trimethoprim.summary: Trimethoprim is an antibiotic used to treat and prevent urinary tract infections such as cystitis, and occasionally other infections. It interferes with folic acid production in bacteria, and the NHS says it is not usually recommended in early pregnancy because it can lower folic acid levels. The NHS lists blood and skin reactions as rare serious side effects that need prompt medical help.

trimethoprim.howItWorks: Trimethoprim works by interfering with the way bacteria make folic acid. Antibiotics such as this act on bacteria and do not work against colds, flu or other viral infections. In the body, a long course can occasionally lower folic acid levels.

common: Itching or a mild rash, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, thrush and headaches are the common effects listed by the NHS.
Being sick or having severe diarrhoea can stop contraceptive pills from protecting against pregnancy.
For headaches, the NHS lists paracetamol and ibuprofen as suitable to take alongside trimethoprim.
serious: Unexplained bruising or bleeding, a sore throat, mouth ulcers or a high temperature can be signs of a blood problem; the NHS says to contact NHS 111 or a doctor straight away.
Serious skin reactions such as blistering or peeling need the same prompt contact with NHS 111 or a doctor.

Bloody or severe diarrhoea, sudden severe stomach pain (a possible sign of pancreatitis) and yellowing of the skin or eyes (a possible sign of liver problems) also need prompt contact with NHS 111 or a doctor.

Signs of meningitis (such as headache, high temperature, stiff neck and sensitivity to bright light), which the NHS describes as very rare, or of high potassium (muscle weakness, an abnormal heartbeat or chest pains) are emergencies: call 999 or go to A&E.
Swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat, or fast or difficult breathing, may signal a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) and needs a 999 call.

Pregnancy and trying to conceive are circumstances where the NHS advises checking with a doctor first.
The NHS says trimethoprim can be taken in pregnancy but is not usually recommended in early pregnancy, because it can lower folic acid levels.
For someone trying to conceive who takes it daily, the NHS says the doctor may change the antibiotic or prescribe high-dose folic acid.
Small amounts pass into breast milk and side effects in the baby are unlikely with short-term use, though a pharmacist, doctor, midwife or health visitor is the person to ask.
Medicines named by the NHS as interacting include rifampicin, warfarin, acenocoumarol, digoxin, phenytoin, repaglinide, pioglitazone and methotrexate.
The NHS says there is not enough information to know whether herbal remedies or supplements can be taken with trimethoprim.
MedlinePlus asks people to tell the prescriber about allergies to trimethoprim or sulfa drugs and about all other medicines, vitamins and supplements.
The NHS says normal eating and drinking can continue during treatment.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment, though it is best not to drink too much.

sections.heading: What is trimethoprim used for?
sections.body: Trimethoprim is an antibiotic, a medicine that treats infections caused by bacteria. The NHS says it is used to treat and to prevent urinary tract infections, such as cystitis. Less often it is used for other infections, including chest infections and acne. NICE guidance on lower urinary tract infection names trimethoprim as one of two first-choice antibiotics, alongside nitrofurantoin. NICE adds that resistance to trimethoprim is high across the country, so it is considered when the individual risk of resistance is low. NICE describes the risk of resistance as more likely to be lower when trimethoprim has not been used in the previous 3 months. In men, NICE notes that trimethoprim can reach useful levels in prostate tissue. Antibiotics do not work against colds, flu or other viral infections, as the NHS points out.

sections.heading: How does trimethoprim work, and why does folic acid come up?
sections.body: Trimethoprim works by interfering with the way bacteria make folic acid. The NHS explains that a long course can occasionally lower folic acid levels in the body. Low folate levels appear on the NHS list of reasons why the medicine may not be suitable. The NHS also notes that the medicine can lower folic acid levels in pregnancy, which is why it is not usually recommended in early pregnancy. An NHS England patient safety case study states that taking trimethoprim in early pregnancy can result in spinal cord malformation in the foetus. For someone trying to conceive who takes the medicine daily, the NHS says the doctor may switch antibiotic or prescribe high-dose folic acid.

sections.heading: What are the side effects, and which need urgent help?
sections.body: The NHS lists itching or a mild rash, feeling or being sick, diarrhoea, thrush and headaches as common effects. Being sick or having severe diarrhoea can stop contraceptive pills from working. Unexplained bruising or bleeding, a sore throat, mouth ulcers or a high temperature can signal a blood problem. Blistering or peeling skin is a serious skin reaction. Bloody or severe diarrhoea, severe stomach pain and yellowing of the skin or eyes also need prompt contact with NHS 111 or a doctor. Signs of meningitis (described by the NHS as very rare), high potassium (muscle weakness, an abnormal heartbeat or chest pains) or a serious allergic reaction, such as swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat, are emergencies: call 999 or go to A&E.

sections.heading: Who needs extra care with trimethoprim?
sections.body: The NHS lists past allergic reactions to trimethoprim or other medicines, liver or kidney problems, low folate levels, porphyria and other blood disorders as reasons the medicine may not suit someone. MedlinePlus also asks people to tell the prescriber about allergies to trimethoprim or sulfa drugs. Pregnancy is another consideration. The NHS says trimethoprim can be taken in pregnancy but is not usually recommended in the early weeks. It says there is no evidence that the medicine affects fertility in men or women. For someone trying to conceive who takes it daily, a doctor may switch antibiotic or prescribe high-dose folic acid. The NHS says small amounts pass into breast milk and that side effects in the baby are unlikely with short-term use.

sections.heading: Trimethoprim with other medicines, alcohol and food
sections.body: The NHS names several medicines that interact with trimethoprim and can raise the chance of side effects. These include rifampicin, warfarin, acenocoumarol, digoxin, phenytoin, repaglinide, pioglitazone and methotrexate. For headaches, the NHS lists paracetamol and ibuprofen as suitable to take with it. For herbal remedies and supplements, the NHS says there is not enough information to know whether they can be taken with it. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment, though it is best not to drink too much. Normal eating and drinking can continue. For sickness, the NHS suggests taking the tablets with or after food. Anyone taking several medicines, or taking vitamins and supplements, is asked by MedlinePlus to tell the prescriber, who may need to adjust doses or watch for side effects.

faqs.q: Can trimethoprim be taken during pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says it can be taken in pregnancy but is not usually recommended in early pregnancy, because it can lower folic acid levels. Anyone who is pregnant or trying to conceive is advised by the NHS to check with a doctor first. A doctor may choose a different antibiotic or prescribe high-dose folic acid.

faqs.q: Why does folic acid matter with trimethoprim?
faqs.a: Trimethoprim interferes with folic acid production in bacteria, and a long course can occasionally lower folic acid levels in the body. Low folate levels are on the NHS list of reasons the medicine may not suit someone, and early pregnancy is a time of particular care.

faqs.q: What side effects need urgent attention?
faqs.a: Unexplained bruising or bleeding, sore throat, mouth ulcers, a high temperature, blistering or peeling skin, severe or bloody diarrhoea and yellow skin or eyes need prompt contact with NHS 111 or a doctor. Swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat, fast or difficult breathing, muscle weakness or an abnormal heartbeat call for 999 or A&E.

faqs.q: Can alcohol be drunk while taking trimethoprim?
faqs.a: The NHS says alcohol can be drunk during treatment, but it is best not to drink too much. It also says normal eating and drinking can continue.

faqs.q: Does trimethoprim help with colds or flu?
faqs.a: No. The NHS notes that antibiotics do not work against colds, flu or other viral infections. Trimethoprim is mainly used to treat and prevent urinary tract infections, and sometimes chest infections and acne.

tamsulosin.summary: Tamsulosin is an alpha blocker prescribed mainly for the urinary difficulties caused by an enlarged prostate gland. It relaxes the muscle around the bladder and prostate so that peeing becomes easier. Dizziness on standing is a known effect, and the NHS asks people to tell the doctor before cataract or glaucoma surgery.

tamsulosin.howItWorks: Tamsulosin belongs to the group of medicines called alpha blockers. In an enlarged prostate it relaxes the muscle around the bladder and the prostate gland, which makes it easier to pee. The NHS says it is sometimes also used to ease the passing of kidney stones.
tamsulosin.onset: The NHS says tamsulosin works best when it is taken long term.

common: The NHS says many people have no side effects or only minor ones, and that side effects often improve as the body gets used to the medicine.
Dizziness, especially when sitting or standing, and ejaculation problems (such as less semen than usual or none) are the main common side effects.
The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery or tools until dizziness has gone, and says alcohol can intensify the dizziness.
serious: The NHS lists fainting as a serious side effect; for serious side effects other than anaphylaxis and Stevens-Johnson syndrome the NHS says to call NHS 111.

A long-lasting, painful erection (priapism) is listed by the NHS as a serious side effect; the NHS priapism page says to call 999 or go to A&E if an erection lasts more than 3 to 4 hours, and the emc leaflet calls it very rare and says it needs immediate medical help.

A serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) can cause a swollen throat or tongue, an itchy raised rash or difficulty breathing; the NHS says to call 999 if anaphylaxis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome is suspected.

cautions: The NHS says most adults aged 18 and over can take tamsulosin, but it is not suitable for everyone, and children are not usually given it unless a specialist children's doctor prescribes it.
People who have had an allergic reaction to tamsulosin or similar medicines such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin or terazosin may not be able to take it.

The NHS also lists orthostatic hypotension (low blood pressure that causes dizziness on standing), severe liver or kidney problems, and fainting while peeing or straight afterwards as reasons it may not be suitable.

People having cataract or glaucoma surgery are asked to tell the doctor in advance that they take tamsulosin, because it can cause complications during the operation; the doctor may ask for it to be stopped beforehand.
Intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, in which the pupil dilates poorly and the iris becomes floppy during eye surgery, is described in emc patient leaflets.
Other alpha blockers and other blood pressure medicines can lower blood pressure too much when taken with tamsulosin.
The NHS advises against taking it with diclofenac, and says paracetamol, codeine and other NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are OK.
The NHS suggests avoiding alcohol in the first few days, until it is clear how the medicine affects a person, because alcohol can increase the risk of side effects.

The NHS says tamsulosin is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough information to know how it affects the baby; for breastfeeding the NHS advises talking to a doctor or pharmacist first.
tamsulosin.monitoring: NICE guidance on lower urinary tract symptoms in men recommends reviewing men who take an alpha blocker after starting it and then at regular intervals.

sections.heading: What is tamsulosin used for?
sections.body:
The NHS describes tamsulosin as a medicine for an enlarged prostate. It is mainly prescribed for the difficulty peeing that an enlarged prostate gland causes. MedlinePlus says it is prescribed for benign prostatic hyperplasia, which can cause trouble urinating, painful urination, or more frequent or urgent urination.

The NHS says tamsulosin is sometimes also used to help kidney stones pass through the urinary tract, and MedlinePlus notes that doctors sometimes use it for kidney stones. NICE guidance on lower urinary tract symptoms in men lists alfuzosin, doxazosin, tamsulosin and terazosin as alpha blocker options for men with moderate to severe symptoms. UK products include prolonged-release capsules and tablets sold under several brand names.

sections.heading: How does tamsulosin work?
sections.body:
Tamsulosin is classed as an alpha blocker. In a man with an enlarged prostate, it relaxes the muscle around the bladder and prostate gland, which makes peeing easier. The NHS says it can also ease the passing of kidney stones in some cases.

The NHS says tamsulosin works best when taken long term. Stopping it suddenly can make the condition worse because symptoms may return, so the NHS says to talk to a doctor about stopping. The NHS also says alcohol can intensify the blood pressure-lowering effect of the medicine.

Other alpha blockers named by the NHS include alfuzosin, doxazosin, terazosin, indoramin and prazosin. The NHS also describes finasteride and dutasteride, which belong to a different group called 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors, and says some people take both types together.

sections.heading: Side effects
sections.body:
The NHS says many people have no side effects or only minor ones, and that side effects often improve as the body gets used to the medicine. The main common effects are dizziness, especially when sitting or standing, and ejaculation problems. The NHS advises against driving, riding a bike or using machinery until dizziness has gone, and says that producing less semen than usual, or none, is a harmless effect.

The NHS lists fainting, a long-lasting painful erection called priapism, and a serious allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) as serious side effects. Anaphylaxis can cause a swollen throat or tongue, an itchy raised rash or difficulty breathing. The NHS says to call 999 if anaphylaxis or Stevens-Johnson syndrome is suspected, and to call NHS 111 for other serious side effects. For a painful erection, the NHS priapism page says to call 999 or go to A&E if it lasts more than 3 to 4 hours. The emc leaflet lists priapism as very rare and says it needs immediate medical help.

If side effects are bothersome, the NHS says the doctor may be able to prescribe a different medicine.

sections.heading: Eye surgery and who needs extra care
sections.body:
The NHS says most adults aged 18 and over can take tamsulosin, though children are not usually given it unless a specialist children's doctor prescribes it. People who have had an allergic reaction to tamsulosin or similar medicines, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin or terazosin, may not be able to take it. The NHS also lists orthostatic hypotension, which is low blood pressure that causes dizziness on standing, severe liver or kidney problems, and a history of fainting while peeing or straight afterwards.

People having cataract or glaucoma surgery are also on the NHS list, because tamsulosin can cause complications during these operations. The emc leaflets describe intraoperative floppy iris syndrome, in which the pupil dilates poorly and the iris becomes floppy during surgery, and advise telling the eye surgeon about tamsulosin so that precautions can be taken. The NHS says to tell the doctor in advance, and that the doctor may ask for tamsulosin to be stopped beforehand.

The NHS says tamsulosin is not usually recommended in pregnancy because there is not enough information to know how it affects the baby. For breastfeeding, the NHS advises talking to a doctor or pharmacist first.

sections.heading: Other medicines and alcohol
sections.body:
The NHS says other alpha blockers, such as doxazosin, alfuzosin, prazosin or terazosin, and other blood pressure medicines can lower blood pressure too much when taken with tamsulosin. It also says some medicines for erectile dysfunction and for HIV may not mix well with tamsulosin.

The NHS advises against taking tamsulosin with diclofenac. It says paracetamol, codeine and other NSAIDs such as ibuprofen are OK to take with it. The NHS says there is not enough information about combining complementary medicines and herbal remedies with tamsulosin, and that they are generally not tested for their effect on other medicines.

The NHS suggests avoiding alcohol in the first few days, until it is clear how the medicine affects a person, because alcohol can increase the risk of side effects. It advises telling the doctor about any other medicines, herbal remedies, vitamins or supplements before starting.

faqs.q: Is tamsulosin used for anything other than an enlarged prostate?
faqs.a: The NHS says it is mainly prescribed for difficulty peeing caused by an enlarged prostate. It is also sometimes used to help kidney stones pass through the urinary tract.

faqs.q: Can tamsulosin be taken for a long time?
faqs.a: The NHS says tamsulosin works best when it is taken long term. A doctor is the person to talk to about how long treatment should continue.

faqs.q: What happens if tamsulosin is stopped suddenly?
faqs.a: The NHS says stopping suddenly can make the condition worse because symptoms may return. A doctor is the person to talk to about stopping or changing treatment.

faqs.q: Does tamsulosin affect eye surgery?
faqs.a: The NHS says tamsulosin can cause complications during cataract or glaucoma surgery. A person due for this surgery tells the doctor about the medicine in advance, and the doctor may ask for it to be stopped beforehand.

faqs.q: Which side effects need urgent help?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 if anaphylaxis is suspected, for example a swollen throat or tongue or difficulty breathing, and to call NHS 111 for other serious side effects such as fainting. For a painful erection, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if it lasts more than 3 to 4 hours.

finasteride.name: Finasteride
finasteride.summary: Finasteride is a tablet that stops testosterone turning into the hormone DHT, used for an enlarged prostate and for male pattern hair loss. The NHS and the MHRA both describe warnings about low mood, depression and suicidal thoughts, and about sexual side effects that can carry on after the medicine is stopped. For hair loss it is available on a private prescription only, not on the NHS.
usedFor: Benign prostate enlargement (an enlarged prostate), for which the NHS says it is available on NHS prescription
Male pattern hair loss, for which the NHS says it can only be obtained on a private prescription
finasteride.howItWorks: Finasteride is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor. It works by stopping testosterone, a sex hormone, from turning into another hormone called dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
finasteride.onset: The NHS says it can take several months to work fully for an enlarged prostate, and some improvement in hair loss may be seen after a few months.

common: The NHS names losing interest in sex and difficulty getting an erection as the most common side effects.
Ejaculation problems are also on the NHS list of common side effects.
These effects usually improve after a while but can sometimes carry on after finasteride is stopped.
serious: The NHS lists low mood (depression) as a rare serious side effect, advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 straight away, and for hair loss advises stopping the medicine straight away if low mood develops. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if there are thoughts of harming oneself. In a mental-health crisis the routes to help are 999 if in immediate danger, NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123, which is free at any time.
The MHRA says finasteride is associated with depression, suicidal thoughts and sexual dysfunction, and that the sexual problems may persist after treatment is stopped.

The NHS advises speaking to a doctor about any lumps, pain or swelling in the chest area or discharge from the nipples, and notes that breast cancer has been reported rarely in men taking finasteride.

The NHS lists anaphylaxis, a serious allergic reaction, as a rare side effect that may need immediate treatment in hospital; swelling of the face, tongue or throat with difficulty breathing is an emergency, so call 999.

cautions: The NHS says most men aged 18 or over can take finasteride, and that it is generally not recommended for women or children.
The NHS asks that a doctor knows about a past allergic reaction to finasteride, a history of depression or thoughts of self-harm, severe bladder problems or liver problems.
Finasteride can affect PSA (prostate-specific antigen) blood test results used to check for prostate cancer, so the NHS says a man needing a PSA test should tell the doctor he takes it.
Hospital information for women says finasteride must not be used in pregnancy or when breastfeeding, and that people taking it must not donate blood.

MedlinePlus (a US source) says touching broken or crushed tablets may harm an unborn baby, and that a woman who is or could be pregnant and touches them should wash the area with soap and water straight away and call a doctor.

The NHS notes that some men taking finasteride have reported test results showing poor sperm quality or infertility, but that this is not a common side effect and sperm quality usually returns to normal after stopping.
The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking finasteride.
The MHRA advises prescribers to ask about any history of depression or suicidal thoughts and to review men on finasteride regularly.
finasteride.monitoring: The MHRA advises prescribers to ask about depression and suicidal thoughts and to review men on finasteride regularly. Suspected side effects can be reported to the MHRA through the Yellow Card scheme.

sections.heading: What is finasteride used for and how does it work?
sections.body: Finasteride is a tablet taken by mouth. The NHS describes two uses: treating an enlarged prostate, which doctors call benign prostate enlargement, and treating male pattern baldness. For an enlarged prostate it is available on an NHS prescription, while for hair loss the NHS says it can only be obtained on a private prescription, so the person pays the full cost. Finasteride is a 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, which means it stops testosterone, a sex hormone, turning into another hormone called DHT. The NHS says it can take several months to work fully for an enlarged prostate, and some improvement in hair loss may be seen after a few months. The NHS says most men aged 18 or over can take it and that it is generally not recommended for women or children. Brand names include Proscar and Propecia. The MHRA has also added a precautionary warning to the product information for dutasteride, a similar medicine, that mood changes have been reported with finasteride, which is in the same class.

sections.heading: What are the sexual side effects of finasteride?
sections.body: The NHS names losing interest in sex and difficulty getting an erection as the main side effects of finasteride. Ejaculation problems are also on its list of common side effects. They usually improve after a while but can sometimes carry on even after finasteride is stopped. Some men have reported that sexual side effects kept bothering them after they stopped taking it. The MHRA drug safety updates make the same point, noting reports of sexual dysfunction that continued after treatment ended. In 2026 the MHRA said the product information for the hair-loss tablet is being updated to state that sexual dysfunction may contribute to mood disorders, and that it has also been reported without any change in mood. Men with concerns about sexual side effects are asked to discuss them with a healthcare professional. The NHS notes that some men taking finasteride have reported test results showing poor sperm quality or infertility, but says this is not a common side effect and that sperm quality usually returns to normal after stopping.

sections.heading: Mood changes, depression and suicidal thoughts
sections.body: The NHS lists low mood, or depression, as a rare side effect of finasteride. The NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for low mood, and for men taking it for hair loss, stopping the medicine straight away. The MHRA says finasteride is associated with depression, suicidal thoughts and sexual dysfunction. Its 2026 update says men who develop depression or suicidal thoughts on the hair-loss tablet should stop it and contact their doctor. The MHRA also advises prescribers to ask about any past depression or suicidal thoughts and to review men regularly. Earlier, it introduced a patient alert card to raise awareness of the possible psychiatric and sexual side effects. The NHS asks that a doctor knows beforehand about a history of depression or thoughts of self-harm. For thoughts of harming oneself, the NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E. In a mental-health crisis the routes to help are 999 if in immediate danger, NHS 111 (mental health option) and Samaritans on 116 123, which is free at any time. Suspected side effects can be reported through the Yellow Card scheme.

sections.heading: PSA tests, breast changes and pregnancy
sections.body: Finasteride can affect the results of a PSA test, a blood test used to check for prostate cancer. The NHS says a man who needs a PSA test should tell the doctor he is taking finasteride. On breast changes, the NHS says to speak to a doctor about any lumps, pain or swelling in the chest area, or discharge from the nipples. The NHS also notes rare reports of breast cancer in men taking finasteride. Hospital information for women says finasteride must not be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding, and that people taking it must not donate blood. MedlinePlus, a US source, says touching broken or crushed tablets may harm an unborn baby. It adds that a woman who is or could be pregnant and touches them should wash the area with soap and water straight away and call a doctor. The NHS says alcohol can be drunk while taking finasteride.

faqs.q: Can finasteride cause depression?
faqs.a: The NHS lists low mood, or depression, as a rare side effect, and the MHRA says finasteride is associated with depression and suicidal thoughts. The NHS advises contacting a doctor or NHS 111 straight away for low mood, stopping straight away if taking it for hair loss, and calling 999 or going to A&E for thoughts of self-harm.

faqs.q: Do the sexual side effects go away after stopping finasteride?
faqs.a: The NHS says side effects usually improve after a while but can sometimes carry on after stopping. The MHRA notes reports of sexual dysfunction that continued after treatment ended, and men with concerns are asked to discuss them with a healthcare professional.

faqs.q: Can women handle finasteride tablets?
faqs.a: MedlinePlus, a US source, says touching broken or crushed tablets may harm an unborn baby. A woman who is or could be pregnant and touches them is advised to wash the area with soap and water straight away and call a doctor.

faqs.q: Does finasteride affect a PSA test?
faqs.a: The NHS says finasteride can affect PSA results, a blood test used to check for prostate cancer. A man who needs the test is asked to tell the doctor he takes it.

faqs.q: Is finasteride for hair loss available on the NHS?
faqs.a: The NHS says finasteride for hair loss can only be obtained on a private prescription, with the person paying the full cost. It is available on NHS prescription for an enlarged prostate.

tetracyclines.name: Tetracyclines
tetracyclines.summary: Tetracyclines are a group of antibiotics that stop bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive. Doxycycline is the member described here, and the NHS lists it for chest, dental and skin infections, rosacea and some sexually transmitted infections.
tetracyclines.mechanism: The NHS explains that doxycycline, a tetracycline antibiotic, stops bacteria from making the proteins they need to survive. For rosacea, the NHS says it mainly reduces inflammation in the skin.
cautions: Not usually used during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or in younger children, because doxycycline can affect how teeth and bones develop, according to the NHS.

A hospital leaflet advises against taking indigestion remedies, or supplements containing iron, calcium, magnesium, aluminium or zinc, at the same time as doxycycline, because they can interfere with absorption.
The NHS says alcohol is best avoided, as it can stop doxycycline working properly.
The NHS says doxycycline can be taken by people allergic to penicillin, because the two are different types of antibiotic.
Some people get thrush after antibiotics, and the NHS suggests asking a pharmacist or doctor if this happens.
classEffects: Headaches, feeling sick and being sick are common side effects of doxycycline.
Skin that is more sensitive to the sun, which can cause a rash, itching and redness.

nitroimidazoles.name: Nitroimidazoles
nitroimidazoles.summary: Antibiotic and antiparasitic medicines, including metronidazole and tinidazole, that act on bacteria and parasites.
nitroimidazoles.mechanism: Microbial enzymes inside susceptible bacteria and parasites activate nitroimidazoles. The activated form then damages proteins and DNA. A study in Giardia found that metronidazole and tinidazole bind to the same subset of proteins.
cautions: For metronidazole, the NHS advises avoiding alcohol during treatment and for 2 days afterwards. Reactions listed include feeling or being sick, stomach pain, hot flushes, a pounding heartbeat and a headache.
NCBI LiverTox describes tinidazole as a nitroimidazole similar to metronidazole, with a likely similar range and frequency of side effects.
Tinidazole is broken down largely in the liver by an enzyme called CYP 3A4, which can lead to significant interactions with other medicines, according to LiverTox.
classEffects: LiverTox says tinidazole causes a low rate of raised liver enzymes during treatment, and rare cases of clinically apparent acute liver injury.

urinary-antibacterials.name: Urinary antibacterials
urinary-antibacterials.summary: Antibiotics used for urinary tract infections. The NHS describes nitrofurantoin as a medicine to treat urinary tract infections such as cystitis, and trimethoprim is also an NHS-described antibiotic for urinary tract infections.
urinary-antibacterials.mechanism: Nitrofurantoin reaches useful concentrations only in urine, so it is used for lower urinary tract infections such as cystitis and is unsuitable for upper infections of the kidneys.
cautions: The NHS lists a past allergic reaction, a lung condition, severe kidney problems, diabetes, anaemia or vitamin B deficiency, and porphyria among the reasons nitrofurantoin may not be suitable.
The NHS says nitrofurantoin can usually be taken in earlier pregnancy, but a doctor may not recommend it later because it can affect the baby's red blood cells.
For trimethoprim, the NHS lists an allergic reaction, liver or kidney problems and blood disorders such as porphyria among the reasons it may not be suitable.
The NHS says trimethoprim can lower folic acid levels and is not usually recommended in early pregnancy.
classEffects: Nausea, diarrhoea, loss of appetite, headaches and dark yellow or brown urine are common side effects of nitrofurantoin, and usually go away when it is stopped.
Itching or a skin rash may occur with trimethoprim, and these effects are usually mild and short-lived, according to the NHS.
Serious reactions to nitrofurantoin, such as swelling of the throat or tongue or difficulty breathing, are rare; the NHS lists these as symptoms of anaphylaxis, which needs a 999 call.

alpha-blockers.name: Alpha blockers
alpha-blockers.summary: Alpha blockers, also called alpha-adrenoreceptor antagonists, are medicines that relax muscle; tamsulosin is used to relax the muscle around the bladder and prostate in an enlarged prostate.
alpha-blockers.mechanism: In an enlarged prostate, tamsulosin relaxes the muscle around the bladder and prostate gland, which makes it easier to pee.
cautions: The NHS says other alpha blockers, such as doxazosin, alfuzosin, prazosin or terazosin, may lower blood pressure, and some blood pressure medicines may not mix well with tamsulosin.
Orthostatic hypotension, low blood pressure causing dizziness on standing, is listed by the NHS as a reason tamsulosin is not suitable.
The NHS also lists severe liver or kidney problems, planned cataract or glaucoma eye surgery and having fainted while urinating or just afterwards among the reasons tamsulosin may not be suitable.
classEffects: Dizziness or light-headedness, which a hospital leaflet notes may occur when first starting tamsulosin.
An allergic reaction to one alpha blocker, such as alfuzosin, doxazosin, prazosin or terazosin, is a reason the NHS lists against tamsulosin.

5-alpha-reductase-inhibitors.name: 5-alpha reductase inhibitors
5-alpha-reductase-inhibitors.summary: A group of medicines that stop testosterone turning into the hormone DHT; finasteride, described by the NHS for an enlarged prostate and male pattern hair loss, is one of them. The MHRA has issued safety warnings about psychiatric side effects and sexual dysfunction for finasteride and dutasteride.
5-alpha-reductase-inhibitors.mechanism: These medicines work by stopping testosterone, a sex hormone, turning into another hormone called dihydrotestosterone (DHT).
classEffects: Sexual side effects such as losing interest in sex and difficulty getting an erection are the main side effects the NHS lists for finasteride, and some men report them continuing after stopping.
The MHRA says finasteride is associated with depression, suicidal thoughts and sexual dysfunction, and has added a precautionary warning for dutasteride.
cautions: Finasteride can affect PSA blood test results, so the NHS advises telling the doctor about it if a PSA test is due.
For depression or suicidal thoughts, MHRA guidance for finasteride is to contact a healthcare professional urgently; if someone is in immediate danger, call 999 or go to A&E.
